title: Lord, have mercy
hook: three short Greek cries left inside the Latin Mass

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Confiteor: through my fault, and a fist on the chest. Your line was we all begin as sinners.

For many centuries, the Mass in the West was said in Latin. The readings, the prayers, the priest's words over the bread. But near the start, right after the confession, the choir or the people would sing three short cries in a completely different language. Not Latin. Greek. It's like finding one line of an old family song, in grandma's language, still sung in the middle of a house where nobody speaks it anymore. It was never put into Latin.
screen: `CENTURIES OF LATIN.` → `ONE MOMENT IN GREEK.` → `NEVER PUT INTO LATIN.`

segments.voice: Kyrie eleison. Lord, have mercy. Christe eleison. Christ, have mercy. Kyrie eleison. Lord, have mercy. Kyrios is Greek for Lord, a title the New Testament gives Jesus. Eleison means have mercy. The cry came into the Roman Mass from the Greek-speaking churches of the East, and when the West prayed in Latin, this piece was kept in its original tongue, like a stitch that holds the two halves of the Church together. For centuries each cry was repeated three times, nine in all. Now it's usually twice each, six in all, and often said or sung in English. And this cry isn't a church invention. It's the cry of desperate people on the road in the Gospels. Two blind men sitting by the road hear Jesus passing, and shout: have mercy on us. A mother from outside Israel, whose daughter is suffering, follows him shouting, in the Douay-Rheims: "Have mercy on me, O Lord, thou son of David." People who had run out of every other option. So the Kyrie at Mass is the whole church standing in their place on the roadside. Dictionaries trace one more thing in the word. The Greek for mercy, eleos, gave a word for giving to the poor, eleēmosynē. That word traveled through Latin into Old English and shrank, over centuries, into our word alms. Mercy that you ask for, and mercy that you give, come from the same root.
screen: `KYRIOS AND ELEISON.` · `KEPT IN GREEK INSIDE THE LATIN.` · `THE CRY FROM THE ROADSIDE.` · `MERCY AND ALMS, ONE ROOT.` · then, large: `HAVE MERCY ON ME, O LORD, THOU SON OF DAVID.`

segments.voice: Breathe in slowly, and on the out-breath, if you pray, say quietly: Kyrie eleison; then Christe eleison on the next, and Kyrie eleison on the third. If you don't pray, you can simply let three slow breaths go, thinking of someone, maybe yourself, who could use mercy today. Then let the quiet stay.
Kyrie eleison. Greek for Lord, have mercy: the cry of the roadside, kept in Greek inside the Latin Mass.
Your line: mercy, three times. A cry from the roadside, still sung near the start of Mass. Day one hundred and six, done.

howItsDone: Near the start of Mass, after the penitential act (or as part of it), the Kyrie is said or sung, usually twice for each line: Lord, have mercy; Christ, have mercy; Lord, have mercy, in English or in the original Greek.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): hook's 'about fifteen hundred years' and 'every word of it' cut (Hebrew Amen, Alleluia and Hosanna stayed, and Good Friday kept another Greek chant); original note no longer calls it 'the one Greek prayer'; kyrios described as the New Testament's title for Jesus; alms etymology marked as what dictionaries trace.
Douay-Rheims Matthew 15:22 fragment given from memory; confirm.
History: the Kyrie probably entered the Roman Mass from Eastern litanies around the 5th–6th century; the script says only that it came from the Greek-speaking churches of the East. Confirm.

'For about fifteen hundred years … in Latin': the Roman Mass was in Latin from roughly the 4th century until the vernacular reforms after Vatican II (1960s). Confirm the round figure. (The Kyrie was not the only non-Latin element: Hebrew words like Amen, Alleluia and Hosanna also stayed; the hook says 'one moment in Greek', which is accurate for Greek.)
Ninefold Kyrie in the pre-1970 rite; GIRM 52: each acclamation ordinarily said twice. Confirm.
Etymology eleos → eleēmosynē → Latin eleemosyna → Old English ælmesse → alms: confirm.
